tagline: Master the legal knowledge NALA tests on the Certified Paralegal exam.

domains.name: United States Legal System
domains.description: Sources of law, the structure of the courts, available remedies, and administrative law.

domains.name: Professional and Ethical Responsibility
domains.description: ABA Model Rules of Professional Conduct and the boundaries of paralegal practice.

domains.name: Civil Litigation
domains.description: Jurisdiction, the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure and Evidence, and alternative dispute resolution.

domains.name: Contracts and Corporate/Commercial Law
domains.description: Contract formation and enforcement plus business organizations and their rights and responsibilities.

domains.description: Core substantive practice areas: criminal law, estates and probate, real property, torts, and bankruptcy.

questions.stem: A paralegal is researching the foundational sources of U.S. law. Which source is the supreme law of the land, to which all other laws must yield?

options.text: The United States Constitution
Federal statutes enacted by Congress
Regulations issued by federal agencies
Decisions of the federal courts of appeals

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Under the Supremacy Clause, the U.S. Constitution is the supreme law of the land; every statute, regulation, and judicial decision must conform to it. Why the others are wrong: **B** statutes are valid only if constitutional; **C** agency regulations derive from and are subordinate to statutes and the Constitution; **D** court decisions interpret the law but are bound by the Constitution.

questions.stem: A trial court in the same jurisdiction is deciding a case whose facts closely match a prior ruling by that state's highest court. Under stare decisis, how should the trial court treat that prior ruling?

options.text: As binding (mandatory) authority it must follow
As merely persuasive authority it may ignore
As dicta with no precedential value
As authority that applies only if both parties agree

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Stare decisis obligates a lower court to follow the holdings of a higher court within the same jurisdiction; a state supreme court ruling is binding on that state's trial courts. Why the others are wrong: **B** decisions of a superior court in the same jurisdiction are mandatory, not merely persuasive; **C** a holding on point is precedent, not dicta; **D** binding precedent applies regardless of the parties' agreement.

questions.stem: A client sues a neighbor seeking a court order requiring the neighbor to tear down a fence that encroaches on the client's land. The client is not asking for money. What type of remedy is this?

options.text: An equitable remedy (injunction)
Compensatory damages
Punitive damages
Liquidated damages

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** An order compelling a party to act or refrain from acting is an injunction, a classic equitable remedy available when money damages are inadequate. Why the others are wrong: **B** compensatory damages are money to cover actual loss, not a court order to act; **C** punitive damages punish wrongdoing and are also monetary; **D** liquidated damages are a contractually fixed sum, not injunctive relief.

questions.stem: A federal agency adopts a new rule after publishing a proposed rule in the Federal Register and inviting public comments. This process reflects which body of law governing how agencies operate?

options.text: Administrative law (notice-and-comment rulemaking under the APA)
Constitutional law
Common law
Admiralty law

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Administrative law governs agency action; the federal Administrative Procedure Act requires notice-and-comment rulemaking, exactly the process described. Why the others are wrong: **B** constitutional law concerns the structure and limits of government power, not agency procedure; **C** common law is judge-made law from case decisions; **D** admiralty law governs maritime matters and is unrelated.

questions.stem: Which court sits at the top of the federal judiciary and serves as the final arbiter of questions of federal law?

options.text: The United States Supreme Court
The United States Courts of Appeals (Circuit Courts)
The United States District Courts
The state supreme courts

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** The U.S. Supreme Court is the highest court in the federal system and has final say on federal-law questions. Why the others are wrong: **B** the courts of appeals are intermediate appellate courts below the Supreme Court; **C** district courts are the federal trial courts at the bottom of the structure; **D** state supreme courts are final only on questions of their own state's law.

questions.stem: A federal district court in the Fifth Circuit confronts an issue squarely decided by the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals, but never addressed by the Fifth Circuit or the U.S. Supreme Court. How must the district court treat the Ninth Circuit's decision?

options.text: As persuasive authority it may consider but is not required to follow
As binding authority it must follow
As authority it is forbidden from citing
As binding only because no other court has ruled

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** A decision of a court of appeals binds only courts within its own circuit; in another circuit it is persuasive, not mandatory. Why the others are wrong: **B** the Ninth Circuit does not bind Fifth Circuit district courts; **C** courts may cite out-of-circuit authority as persuasive; **D** absence of local precedent does not convert persuasive authority into binding authority.

questions.stem: Which two of the following are equitable remedies rather than remedies at law? (Select two.)

options.text: Specific performance
Compensatory money damages
A permanent injunction
Nominal money damages

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, C):** Specific performance (an order to perform a contract) and injunctions are equitable remedies a court grants when monetary relief is inadequate. Why the others are wrong: **B** compensatory damages are the classic legal (money) remedy; **D** nominal damages are also a money remedy at law, awarded when a right is violated without substantial loss.

questions.stem: At a social gathering, a friend asks a paralegal whether she should sue her landlord and what her chances are. What is the proper response under the rules governing the unauthorized practice of law?

options.text: The paralegal must decline to give legal advice and may refer the friend to an attorney
The paralegal may advise the friend because it is an informal, non-billable setting
The paralegal may give advice as long as a disclaimer is added
The paralegal may quote the likely outcome but not a recommended course of action

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Giving legal advice is the practice of law; a paralegal who does so commits UPL, so the proper course is to decline and refer the person to a lawyer. Why the others are wrong: **B** an informal or unpaid setting does not authorize legal advice; **C** a disclaimer cannot cure UPL; **D** assessing the merits or likely outcome is itself legal advice.

questions.stem: A prospective client meets with a paralegal at a law firm to discuss a possible representation. The firm ultimately declines the case. Under the ABA Model Rules, what is the paralegal's duty regarding what the prospective client disclosed?

options.text: Keep the information confidential, because the duty of confidentiality extends to prospective clients
Freely discuss it, since no representation was formed
Disclose it only to opposing counsel if asked
Keep it confidential only if a written fee agreement was signed

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Under Model Rule 1.18, information learned from a prospective client is protected even if no representation results, and that duty flows to the firm's paralegals. Why the others are wrong: **B** the duty attaches to consultations, not only completed engagements; **C** disclosing protected information to opposing counsel would breach confidentiality; **D** confidentiality does not depend on a signed fee agreement.

questions.stem: A paralegal previously worked at Firm A, where she helped defend Acme Corp. She now joins Firm B, which represents a plaintiff suing Acme on the same matter. What is the most appropriate way for Firm B to address this conflict?

options.text: Screen the paralegal from the matter and avoid sharing related fees with her
Do nothing, because conflict rules apply only to attorneys
Have the paralegal continue but instruct her not to discuss the case
Withdraw from all of Firm B's unrelated cases

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** A nonlawyer who switched sides should be timely screened from the matter and not apportioned part of the fee, which generally lets the new firm avoid imputed disqualification. Why the others are wrong: **B** imputed-conflict principles extend to nonlawyer staff; **C** an informal instruction is not an effective screen; **D** withdrawing from unrelated cases does nothing to cure this specific conflict.

questions.stem: A supervising attorney signs and files a discovery response without reviewing the work product an experienced paralegal prepared, and the response contains a material misstatement. Under the ABA Model Rules, who bears professional responsibility?

options.text: The attorney, who must make reasonable efforts to ensure the paralegal's work conforms to the rules and remains responsible for it
The paralegal alone, because the paralegal drafted it
No one, because paralegals are not bound by the Model Rules
The client, for failing to catch the error

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Model Rule 5.3 requires a supervising lawyer to make reasonable efforts to ensure nonlawyer conduct is compatible with the lawyer's obligations; the lawyer cannot delegate away responsibility for the filing. Why the others are wrong: **B** the attorney's supervisory duty is non-delegable; **C** lawyers are accountable for staff work even though the rules bind lawyers directly; **D** the client bears no professional-responsibility duty here.

questions.stem: Which two activities, if performed by a paralegal, would constitute the unauthorized practice of law? (Select two.)

options.text: Setting the fee the firm will charge a new client
Summarizing deposition transcripts for the supervising attorney
Accepting a new case on behalf of the firm and forming the attorney-client relationship
Drafting a discovery request for the attorney's review and signature

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, C):** Setting fees and accepting cases (establishing the attorney-client relationship) are reserved to lawyers; a paralegal doing either engages in UPL. Why the others are wrong: **B** summarizing depositions is proper delegated work under attorney supervision; **D** drafting documents for an attorney's review and signature is permissible paralegal work, not UPL.

questions.stem: A citizen of Texas sues a citizen of California for $200,000 in a state-law breach-of-contract claim. On what basis may the case be filed in federal court?

options.text: Diversity jurisdiction, because the parties are citizens of different states and the amount in controversy exceeds $75,000
Federal-question jurisdiction, because all contract disputes raise federal questions
Supplemental jurisdiction, which can stand on its own
There is no basis; contract suits must be filed in state court

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Diversity jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. 1332 requires complete diversity of citizenship and an amount in controversy exceeding $75,000, both satisfied here. Why the others are wrong: **B** an ordinary state-law contract claim raises no federal question; **C** supplemental jurisdiction attaches to claims related to an existing federal claim and cannot stand alone; **D** diversity provides a valid federal basis, so state court is not the only option.

questions.stem: Under the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, after being served with a complaint in the typical case (no waiver of service), how many days does a defendant generally have to file an answer?

options.text: 21 days
10 days
45 days
90 days

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** FRCP 12(a)(1)(A)(i) gives a defendant 21 days after being served to serve an answer (60 days if the defendant timely waived service). Why the others are wrong: **B** 10 days is not the federal answer deadline; **C** 45 days is not the rule absent special circumstances; **D** 90 days is the presumptive outer limit for serving process under Rule 4(m), not the time to answer.

questions.stem: At trial, a party offers a witness's out-of-court statement to prove the truth of the matter asserted. Opposing counsel objects on hearsay grounds. Under the Federal Rules of Evidence, the statement is generally:

options.text: Inadmissible unless it falls within an exception or exclusion to the hearsay rule
Always admissible because the witness is available to testify
Admissible only if it was made under oath
Inadmissible in all circumstances, with no exceptions

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Under FRE 801-802, an out-of-court statement offered for its truth is hearsay and inadmissible unless a recognized exception or exclusion applies. Why the others are wrong: **B** the declarant's availability does not by itself defeat the hearsay bar; **C** being made under oath is not the test for hearsay admissibility; **D** the rules contain numerous exceptions, so a blanket bar is incorrect.

questions.stem: Two parties agree to submit their dispute to a neutral third party who will hear evidence and render a binding decision they have agreed to accept. Which form of alternative dispute resolution is this?

options.text: Binding arbitration
Mediation
Early neutral evaluation
A settlement conference

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** In binding arbitration a neutral arbitrator hears the dispute and issues a decision (award) the parties have agreed to be bound by. Why the others are wrong: **B** a mediator facilitates negotiation but cannot impose a decision; **C** early neutral evaluation gives a non-binding assessment of the case; **D** a settlement conference is a negotiation, not a binding adjudication.

questions.stem: A defendant files a Rule 12(b)(6) motion to dismiss for failure to state a claim. In ruling on the motion, how must the court treat the factual allegations in the complaint?

options.text: Accept the well-pleaded factual allegations as true and ask whether they state a plausible claim
Weigh the evidence and decide which side is more credible
Require the plaintiff to prove the allegations by a preponderance of the evidence
Dismiss only if the plaintiff failed to attach documentary exhibits

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** On a Rule 12(b)(6) motion the court accepts well-pleaded facts as true and tests whether the complaint states a plausible claim for relief. Why the others are wrong: **B** the court does not weigh evidence or credibility at the pleading stage; **C** no proof is required to survive a motion to dismiss, only sufficient allegations; **D** there is no general requirement to attach exhibits to a complaint.

questions.stem: A paralegal is organizing discovery for a federal case. Which of the following is a discovery device under the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure?

options.text: Interrogatories served on another party
A jury instruction
A notice of appeal
A closing argument

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Interrogatories (FRCP 33) are written questions served on a party and answered under oath; they are a core discovery device. Why the others are wrong: **B** a jury instruction guides the jury at trial, not a discovery tool; **C** a notice of appeal is a post-judgment filing; **D** a closing argument is part of trial advocacy, not discovery.

questions.stem: Place the following stages of a typical federal civil lawsuit in the correct chronological order, from earliest to latest.

options.text: Filing the complaint
Discovery
Trial
Appeal

questions.explanation: A civil action begins when the plaintiff files the complaint (A) to commence the suit. After the pleadings, the parties exchange information through discovery (B). If the case is not resolved by motion or settlement, it proceeds to trial (C), where the merits are decided. A party dissatisfied with the judgment may then seek appeal (D) to a higher court. This pleading-to-discovery-to-trial-to-appeal sequence is the standard litigation lifecycle.

questions.stem: A paralegal is reviewing whether a valid contract was formed. Which three elements are generally required for an enforceable contract?

options.text: Offer, acceptance, and consideration
Offer, notarization, and recording
Writing, witnesses, and a seal
Negotiation, mediation, and signature

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** A contract generally requires a valid offer, an acceptance of that offer, and consideration (a bargained-for exchange) supported by capacity and legality. Why the others are wrong: **B** notarization and recording are not general formation elements; **C** most contracts need no writing, witnesses, or seal to be valid; **D** mediation is dispute resolution, not a formation element.

questions.stem: Under the Statute of Frauds, which of the following contracts generally must be in writing to be enforceable?

options.text: A contract for the sale of an interest in land
A contract to paint a house next week
An agreement to buy a $40 lamp
An oral agreement to mow a lawn this weekend

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** The Statute of Frauds requires a writing for contracts transferring an interest in land. Why the others are wrong: **B** a short-term service contract performable within a year need not be written; **C** a sale of goods under $500 falls below the UCC writing threshold; **D** an oral agreement for a weekend service is enforceable because it can be performed within one year.

questions.stem: Article 2 of the Uniform Commercial Code governs which type of transaction?

options.text: The sale of goods (movable, tangible items)
The sale of real estate
Personal-service employment contracts
The licensing of patents

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** UCC Article 2 applies to transactions in goods—things movable and tangible at the time of identification to the contract. Why the others are wrong: **B** real estate is governed by common law and real-property statutes, not Article 2; **C** personal-service contracts are governed by common law; **D** intellectual-property licensing falls outside Article 2's scope.

questions.stem: A homeowner promises to pay a contractor a $5,000 bonus to finish a renovation by a certain date, but the contractor is already contractually bound to finish by that same date. Is the bonus promise enforceable?

options.text: No, because the contractor gave no new consideration under the pre-existing duty rule
Yes, because any promise to pay money is automatically binding
Yes, because the contractor's existing obligation counts as fresh consideration
No, because bonus promises are always illegal

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Under the pre-existing duty rule, performing an obligation one is already bound to perform is not valid consideration, so the bonus promise lacks consideration and is unenforceable. Why the others are wrong: **B** a promise needs consideration to be binding; **C** an existing duty is precisely what fails as consideration; **D** bonus promises are lawful—the defect is the missing consideration, not illegality.

questions.stem: Which business entity is characterized by limited liability for its owners (shareholders) and potential double taxation of corporate profits and dividends?

options.text: A C corporation
A general partnership
A sole proprietorship
A limited liability partnership formed only for professionals

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** A C corporation gives shareholders limited liability and is taxed as a separate entity, so profits are taxed at the corporate level and again as dividends—classic double taxation. Why the others are wrong: **B** general partners face unlimited personal liability and pass-through taxation; **C** a sole proprietor has unlimited liability and pass-through taxation; **D** an LLP provides liability protection but generally pass-through (single-level) taxation.

questions.stem: What is the primary liability advantage of forming a limited liability company (LLC) for its members?

options.text: Members are generally not personally liable for the debts and obligations of the LLC
Members are personally liable for all company debts
The LLC cannot be sued because it is not a legal person
Members must always be taxed as a C corporation

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** An LLC is a separate legal entity, so members' personal assets are generally shielded from the company's debts and liabilities. Why the others are wrong: **B** the whole point of an LLC is to avoid personal liability for company debts; **C** an LLC is a legal entity that can sue and be sued; **D** LLCs have flexible tax treatment and default to pass-through taxation, not mandatory C-corp status.

questions.stem: A buyer and seller have a written contract for custom machinery. The buyer later claims they orally agreed the seller would also provide free annual maintenance, a term absent from the signed writing the parties intended as their final, complete agreement. What doctrine most likely bars that oral term?

options.text: The parol evidence rule
The doctrine of promissory estoppel
The mailbox rule
The doctrine of frustration of purpose

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** The parol evidence rule bars prior or contemporaneous oral agreements that contradict or add to a writing the parties intended as a complete and final integration. Why the others are wrong: **B** promissory estoppel enforces reliance on a promise lacking consideration, not relevant here; **C** the mailbox rule governs when acceptance is effective; **D** frustration of purpose excuses performance when an event destroys the contract's purpose.

questions.stem: One party to a contract clearly indicates, before performance is due, that it will not perform its obligations. This is best described as:

options.text: Anticipatory repudiation, which may allow the other party to treat it as a breach
Substantial performance
An accord and satisfaction
A novation

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Anticipatory repudiation occurs when a party unequivocally announces before the performance date that it will not perform, letting the other party treat the contract as breached and sue immediately. Why the others are wrong: **B** substantial performance is good-faith near-complete performance, the opposite of repudiation; **C** accord and satisfaction settles a disputed obligation; **D** novation substitutes a new party or contract by agreement.

questions.stem: Which two of the following are valid defenses to the enforcement of a contract? (Select two.)

options.text: Fraud in the inducement
Duress
The presence of consideration
A clear, mutual offer and acceptance

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** Fraud and duress are recognized contract defenses; each shows the assent was not genuine, making the contract voidable. Why the others are wrong: **C** consideration is a requirement that supports enforcement, not a defense against it; **D** a clear offer and acceptance helps form a contract rather than defeat it.

questions.stem: A paralegal is summarizing the elements of a negligence claim. Which set correctly lists the four elements?

options.text: Duty, breach, causation, and damages
Offer, acceptance, consideration, and capacity
Intent, act, causation, and harm
Mens rea, actus reus, concurrence, and causation

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** A negligence claim requires a duty of care, breach of that duty, causation (actual and proximate), and resulting damages. Why the others are wrong: **B** these are contract-formation elements; **C** intent is the hallmark of intentional torts, not negligence; **D** mens rea and actus reus are elements of criminal liability.

questions.stem: A manufacturer sells a defectively designed product that injures a consumer who used it as intended. Under the majority approach, the manufacturer may be held liable without any showing of negligence under which theory?

options.text: Strict products liability
Breach of an express warranty only
Intentional infliction of emotional distress
Defamation

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Strict products liability holds a commercial seller liable for harm caused by a defective product regardless of fault or negligence. Why the others are wrong: **B** an express warranty requires a specific affirmation of fact, which need not exist here; **C** intentional infliction requires extreme, intentional conduct causing severe distress; **D** defamation concerns false statements harming reputation, unrelated to product defects.

questions.stem: A person dies without a valid will. How is the decedent's property distributed?

options.text: According to the state's intestate-succession statutes
Entirely to the state by default
According to whatever the funeral home directs
Equally among all of the decedent's friends

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** When a person dies intestate (without a valid will), the estate passes according to the state's intestate-succession statutes, which prioritize spouses and blood relatives. Why the others are wrong: **B** property escheats to the state only when no eligible heirs exist; **C** a funeral home has no authority over estate distribution; **D** friends are not statutory heirs and do not inherit by intestacy.

questions.stem: Under the majority approach, what is generally required for a will to be validly executed?

options.text: It must be in writing, signed by the testator, and witnessed by the required number of competent witnesses
It must be notarized but need not be signed
It must be recorded with the county before death
It must be filed with the IRS

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** A formal will generally must be in writing, signed by the testator (or by another at the testator's direction), and attested by the statutorily required witnesses. Why the others are wrong: **B** notarization does not substitute for the testator's signature; **C** wills are typically not recorded before death; **D** a will is not filed with the IRS as a condition of validity.

questions.stem: Two people take title to real property as joint tenants with right of survivorship. One of them dies. What happens to the deceased co-owner's interest?

options.text: It passes automatically to the surviving joint tenant by operation of law
It passes through the deceased's will to the named beneficiary
It passes to the deceased's heirs by intestacy
It is sold and the proceeds go to the state

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** In a joint tenancy with right of survivorship, the deceased's share passes automatically to the surviving joint tenant outside of probate. Why the others are wrong: **B** the survivorship right overrides the will, so the property does not pass by devise; **C** for the same reason it does not pass by intestacy; **D** there is no forced sale or escheat where a surviving joint tenant exists.

questions.stem: Which document is used to transfer ownership of real property from a seller to a buyer?

options.text: A deed
A promissory note
A complaint
A subpoena

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** A deed is the written instrument that conveys title to real property from grantor to grantee. Why the others are wrong: **B** a promissory note is a promise to repay a debt, not a transfer of title; **C** a complaint initiates a lawsuit; **D** a subpoena commands a person to testify or produce documents.

questions.stem: In a criminal prosecution, what is the standard of proof the government must meet to convict a defendant?

options.text: Beyond a reasonable doubt
A preponderance of the evidence
Clear and convincing evidence
Probable cause

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** To obtain a criminal conviction, the prosecution must prove every element beyond a reasonable doubt—the highest burden in the law. Why the others are wrong: **B** preponderance is the civil standard; **C** clear and convincing is an intermediate standard used in some civil matters; **D** probable cause is the lower threshold for arrest or charging, not for conviction.

questions.stem: Police conduct a search of a home without a warrant, consent, or any recognized exception, and seize evidence. Under the exclusionary rule, how is that evidence generally treated at trial?

options.text: It is generally inadmissible against the defendant in the prosecution's case-in-chief
It is admissible because the police acted in good faith by definition
It is admissible if the crime is serious enough
It must be destroyed and the charges dismissed automatically

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** The exclusionary rule generally bars evidence obtained through a Fourth Amendment violation from the prosecution's case-in-chief. Why the others are wrong: **B** an unjustified warrantless search is not automatically good-faith conduct; **C** the seriousness of the offense does not validate an unconstitutional search; **D** exclusion suppresses the evidence but does not require destruction or automatic dismissal of charges.

questions.stem: An individual debtor files a bankruptcy petition seeking to liquidate non-exempt assets and discharge most unsecured debts. Which chapter of the Bankruptcy Code is this?

options.text: Chapter 7
Chapter 11
Chapter 13
Chapter 9

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Chapter 7 is liquidation bankruptcy: a trustee sells the debtor's non-exempt assets and most remaining unsecured debts are discharged. Why the others are wrong: **B** Chapter 11 is reorganization, used chiefly by businesses; **C** Chapter 13 is a wage-earner repayment plan, not liquidation; **D** Chapter 9 is for municipalities.

questions.stem: Immediately upon the filing of a bankruptcy petition, what protection arises to halt most collection efforts against the debtor?

options.text: The automatic stay
A writ of execution
A mechanic's lien
A deficiency judgment

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Filing a bankruptcy petition triggers the automatic stay, which immediately halts most collection actions, lawsuits, and foreclosures against the debtor. Why the others are wrong: **B** a writ of execution enforces a judgment, the opposite of a stay; **C** a mechanic's lien secures payment for labor or materials; **D** a deficiency judgment is entered against a debtor for a shortfall after collateral is sold.

questions.stem: A creditor wants priority to be paid from specific collateral ahead of other creditors if the debtor defaults. Under UCC Article 9, what must the creditor generally do to make its security interest effective against third parties?

options.text: Perfect the security interest, commonly by filing a financing statement
Record a deed in the county land records
Obtain a default judgment first
File a motion to compel

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** A secured creditor perfects its interest—often by filing a UCC-1 financing statement—to establish priority against other creditors in the collateral. Why the others are wrong: **B** recording a deed concerns real-property title, not Article 9 personal-property security; **C** a security interest does not require a prior judgment; **D** a motion to compel is a discovery tool, unrelated to perfection.

questions.stem: A defendant takes another's property by threatening immediate physical harm to the victim. Which crime most precisely describes this conduct?

options.text: Robbery
Larceny
Burglary
Embezzlement

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Robbery is larceny accomplished by force or by threat of immediate harm to the victim, exactly what is described. Why the others are wrong: **B** larceny is the wrongful taking of property without the element of force or threat; **C** burglary is the unlawful entry of a structure with intent to commit a crime inside; **D** embezzlement is the fraudulent conversion of property lawfully entrusted to the defendant.

questions.stem: Under the majority comparative-negligence approach, what is the effect when a plaintiff is found partly at fault for her own injuries?

options.text: Her recovery is reduced in proportion to her share of fault
She is automatically barred from any recovery
Her fault is irrelevant to the award
The defendant pays double damages

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Under comparative negligence, the plaintiff's damages are reduced by her percentage of fault rather than eliminated. Why the others are wrong: **B** total bar is the old contributory-negligence rule, now the minority view; **C** the plaintiff's fault directly affects the award under comparative negligence; **D** there is no double-damages rule for shared fault.

questions.stem: A grantor transfers property to a trustee to hold and manage for the benefit of a named beneficiary. What is the role of the trustee?

options.text: To hold legal title and manage the trust property as a fiduciary for the beneficiary
To hold both legal and equitable title for the trustee's own benefit
To serve as the beneficiary's litigation attorney
To act as the probate judge over the estate

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** A trustee holds legal title to trust property and owes fiduciary duties to manage it for the beneficiary, who holds equitable title. Why the others are wrong: **B** the trustee does not hold the beneficial (equitable) interest for personal benefit; **C** a trustee serves no role as the beneficiary's litigation counsel; **D** a trustee is not a judge and has no adjudicative authority over the estate.

questions.stem: A landowner grants a utility company the right to run power lines across a strip of the landowner's property, without transferring ownership of the land. What interest has the utility received?

options.text: An easement
A fee simple absolute
A leasehold of the entire parcel
A life estate

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** An easement is a non-possessory right to use another's land for a specific purpose, such as running utility lines. Why the others are wrong: **B** a fee simple absolute is full ownership, which was not transferred; **C** a leasehold gives possession of property for a term, broader than a limited right of use; **D** a life estate is an ownership interest measured by a life, not a limited use right.

questions.stem: Which two of the following are intentional torts rather than negligence-based claims? (Select two.)

options.text: Battery
False imprisonment
A slip-and-fall caused by a wet floor the owner failed to address
A car accident caused by a distracted driver

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** Battery (intentional harmful or offensive contact) and false imprisonment (intentional unlawful confinement) are intentional torts requiring intent. Why the others are wrong: **C** an unaddressed wet floor sounds in negligence (breach of a duty of care), not intent; **D** a distracted-driver collision is likewise a negligence claim, not an intentional tort.

questions.stem: A secured lender holds a mortgage on the borrower's home. The borrower stops making payments. What legal process allows the lender to force a sale of the home to satisfy the debt?

options.text: Foreclosure
Escheat
Adverse possession
Eminent domain

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Foreclosure is the legal process by which a secured lender forces the sale of mortgaged property to satisfy the defaulted debt. Why the others are wrong: **B** escheat transfers property to the state when there are no heirs; **C** adverse possession lets an occupant gain title through long, hostile possession; **D** eminent domain is the government's power to take private property for public use with compensation.

questions.stem: A paralegal is classifying primary sources of law. Which of the following is a primary source rather than a secondary source?

options.text: A law review article analyzing a recent decision
A statute enacted by a state legislature
A legal encyclopedia entry
An American Law Reports (ALR) annotation

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Primary sources are the law itself, such as constitutions, statutes, regulations, and case law; an enacted statute is a primary authority. Why the others are wrong: **A** a law review article only comments on the law, making it secondary; **C** a legal encyclopedia explains and summarizes the law as a secondary source; **D** an ALR annotation collects and analyzes cases but is secondary, not the law itself.

questions.stem: A federal statute and a valid federal regulation both clearly conflict with a state statute on the same subject within Congress's power. Which authority controls?

options.text: The state statute, because states retain police powers
Whichever law was enacted most recently
The federal law, under the Supremacy Clause and preemption
Neither, until a court consolidates them

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Under the Supremacy Clause, valid federal law preempts conflicting state law, so the federal statute and regulation control. Why the others are wrong: **A** police powers do not let a state override valid federal law in a conflict; **B** recency does not resolve a federal-state conflict, supremacy does; **D** the conflict is resolved by preemption, not by waiting for consolidation.

questions.stem: A litigant who lost before a federal administrative agency wants a court to review the agency's decision. Under administrative law, what must the litigant generally do before seeking judicial review?

options.text: Exhaust available administrative remedies within the agency
File directly with the U.S. Supreme Court
Obtain the agency's written consent to be sued
Wait until the same issue arises in another case

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** The exhaustion doctrine generally requires a party to pursue and complete the agency's own review process before a court will hear the matter. Why the others are wrong: **B** review begins in the appropriate lower court, not directly in the Supreme Court; **C** an agency's consent is not a prerequisite to statutory judicial review; **D** review depends on exhausting remedies, not on the issue recurring elsewhere.

questions.stem: A court's published opinion includes a statement about a hypothetical situation not actually before the court and not necessary to its decision. What is this statement called, and what is its precedential weight?

options.text: The holding, which is binding precedent
Dictum, which is not binding but may be persuasive
A concurrence, which controls the outcome
A syllabus, which is binding on lower courts

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Statements unnecessary to the decision are dicta; they do not bind later courts but may be cited as persuasive. Why the others are wrong: **A** the holding is the rule essential to the outcome and is the binding part, unlike dicta; **C** a concurrence agrees in result but does not establish the controlling rule by itself; **D** a syllabus is an editorial summary and is not itself binding law.

questions.stem: A dispute turns purely on the meaning of a state's own statute, with no federal issue involved. Which court is the final authority on what that statute means?

options.text: The United States Supreme Court
The federal court of appeals for that region
That state's highest court
A federal district court sitting in that state

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** A state's highest court is the final arbiter of the meaning of that state's own law. Why the others are wrong: **A** the U.S. Supreme Court is final on federal questions, not on pure state-law meaning; **B** a federal court of appeals must defer to the state high court on state-law interpretation; **D** a federal district court likewise follows the state high court's reading of state law.

questions.stem: Which two of the following are equitable remedies a court may grant when monetary damages are inadequate? (Select two.)

options.text: Rescission of a contract
Punitive damages
Reformation of a written instrument
Compensatory damages

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, C):** Rescission (undoing a contract) and reformation (rewriting a writing to reflect the true agreement) are equitable remedies used when money relief is inadequate. Why the others are wrong: **B** punitive damages are a monetary (legal) remedy meant to punish; **D** compensatory damages are the classic legal remedy of money to cover loss.

questions.stem: A paralegal answers the firm's phone, and a caller asks to speak with the attorney about starting a new lawsuit. The attorney is unavailable. What may the paralegal properly tell the caller?

options.text: That the firm will take the case and the caller is now a client
An estimate of how likely the caller is to win
That she will relay the message and schedule a consultation with the attorney
The fee the firm will charge for the matter

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Relaying messages and scheduling appointments are administrative tasks a paralegal may perform without engaging in the practice of law. Why the others are wrong: **A** accepting a case and forming the attorney-client relationship is reserved to the attorney; **B** predicting the outcome is giving legal advice, which is UPL; **D** setting fees is a lawyer's responsibility, not the paralegal's.

questions.stem: A client tells a paralegal in confidence that he plans to hide assets to avoid a court judgment. Under the duty of confidentiality, what is the paralegal's proper course?

options.text: Promptly inform the supervising attorney and keep the information confidential from outsiders
Post about it anonymously to warn the public
Tell opposing counsel to be transparent
Ignore it because confidentiality forbids telling anyone, including the attorney

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** The paralegal works under the attorney and should report client information to the supervising lawyer, who decides how to handle it, while keeping it confidential from outside parties. Why the others are wrong: **B** disclosing client information publicly breaches confidentiality; **C** revealing it to opposing counsel is an improper disclosure; **D** confidentiality protects against outside disclosure, not communication within the legal team.

questions.stem: Under the attorney-client privilege as generally applied, which communication is protected from compelled disclosure?

options.text: A confidential communication between the client and the attorney's paralegal made to obtain legal advice
A statement the client made to a friend at dinner about the case
Underlying facts the client personally witnessed, which the client may be compelled to testify about
A communication made for the purpose of committing a future crime or fraud

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** The privilege covers confidential communications between client and the lawyer's team (including paralegals) made to obtain legal advice. Why the others are wrong: **B** disclosing the communication to a non-team friend defeats confidentiality, so no privilege attaches; **C** the privilege protects communications, not the underlying facts, which a witness can be compelled to disclose; **D** the crime-fraud exception removes protection for communications furthering a future crime or fraud.

questions.stem: A paralegal drafting a pleading discovers controlling authority directly against the client's position. Under the duty of candor reflected in the Model Rules, what should the paralegal do?

options.text: Conceal the adverse authority from the supervising attorney
Bring the adverse controlling authority to the supervising attorney's attention
Decide independently to omit it from the brief
Cite it as if it supports the client

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** A paralegal supports the lawyer's duty of candor to the tribunal by flagging directly adverse controlling authority so the attorney can address it. Why the others are wrong: **A** concealing it undermines the candor obligation and the attorney's ability to comply; **C** the decision on disclosure belongs to the attorney, not the paralegal acting alone; **D** misrepresenting authority is dishonest and violates the duty of candor.

questions.stem: A paralegal works under a supervising attorney. Which two activities are permissible for the paralegal rather than the unauthorized practice of law? (Select two.)

options.text: Conducting legal research and drafting a memorandum for the attorney
Appearing in court to argue a motion on the client's behalf
Interviewing a witness and preparing a summary for the attorney
Advising the client which settlement offer to accept

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, C):** Legal research, drafting for attorney review, and witness interviews are proper delegated tasks performed under attorney supervision. Why the others are wrong: **B** appearing and arguing in court is representing a client, reserved to licensed attorneys; **D** advising which offer to accept is rendering legal advice, which is UPL.

questions.stem: A plaintiff sues an out-of-state defendant. The defendant has never set foot in the forum state but operates an interactive website through which it regularly sells and ships products to forum residents. What concept determines whether the forum may exercise personal jurisdiction?

options.text: Whether the defendant has sufficient minimum contacts with the forum so that jurisdiction is consistent with due process
Whether the amount in controversy exceeds $75,000
Whether the claim arises under federal law
Whether venue is proper in the district

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Personal jurisdiction over a nonresident turns on minimum contacts such that suit does not offend traditional notions of fair play and substantial justice. Why the others are wrong: **B** the amount in controversy goes to diversity subject-matter jurisdiction, not personal jurisdiction; **C** a federal question concerns subject-matter jurisdiction; **D** venue addresses which district is appropriate, a separate question from personal jurisdiction.

questions.stem: After the close of discovery, a defendant moves for summary judgment under FRCP 56. What must the defendant show to be entitled to judgment?

options.text: That the jury is likely to find the defendant more credible
That there is no genuine dispute of material fact and the movant is entitled to judgment as a matter of law
That the plaintiff failed to attach exhibits to the complaint
That the complaint omitted a demand for a jury trial

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Summary judgment is proper only when there is no genuine dispute of material fact and the moving party is entitled to judgment as a matter of law. Why the others are wrong: **A** the court does not weigh credibility on summary judgment; **C** there is no general requirement to attach exhibits to a complaint; **D** failing to demand a jury does not entitle a party to summary judgment.

questions.stem: At trial in a civil case, the plaintiff offers a properly authenticated photocopy of a signed contract. The opponent objects, demanding the original. Under the Federal Rules of Evidence best evidence (original document) rule, the duplicate is:

options.text: Generally admissible to the same extent as the original unless a genuine question is raised about authenticity or fairness
Never admissible because only originals may be used
Admissible only if notarized
Admissible only in criminal cases

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Under FRE 1003, a duplicate is admissible to the same extent as an original unless a genuine question of authenticity is raised or admission would be unfair. Why the others are wrong: **B** the rule expressly permits duplicates, so an absolute originals-only bar is wrong; **C** notarization is not the standard for admitting a duplicate; **D** the rule applies in civil and criminal proceedings alike.

questions.stem: A defendant believes the plaintiff's claim arises from the same transaction as a claim the defendant has against the plaintiff. Under the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, how should the defendant generally raise that claim, or risk waiving it?

options.text: As a compulsory counterclaim in the answer
As a separate later lawsuit, with no risk of waiver
Only after the plaintiff wins at trial
By a motion to dismiss the plaintiff's complaint

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Under FRCP 13(a), a claim arising from the same transaction or occurrence as the opposing party's claim is a compulsory counterclaim that generally must be pleaded or it is waived. Why the others are wrong: **B** saving it for a later suit risks losing it because it is compulsory; **C** the counterclaim is raised in the responsive pleading, not after trial; **D** a motion to dismiss attacks the complaint and does not assert the defendant's own claim.

questions.stem: A paralegal needs to compel a non-party witness to appear at a deposition and bring specified documents. Which instrument accomplishes this?

options.text: A subpoena duces tecum
A complaint
A request for admission
A motion in limine

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** A subpoena duces tecum commands a non-party to appear and produce designated documents or things. Why the others are wrong: **B** a complaint initiates a lawsuit and does not compel a witness; **C** a request for admission is served on a party to admit or deny facts, not to compel a non-party's attendance; **D** a motion in limine seeks a pretrial ruling on the admissibility of evidence.

questions.stem: Which two statements correctly distinguish mediation from binding arbitration? (Select two.)

options.text: A mediator helps the parties reach their own voluntary agreement but cannot impose a result
In binding arbitration the neutral issues a decision the parties have agreed to be bound by
A mediator renders a binding judgment enforceable like a court order
Arbitration is always non-binding and merely advisory

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** A mediator facilitates a voluntary settlement without power to impose one, whereas a binding arbitrator issues an award the parties agreed to accept. Why the others are wrong: **C** a mediator cannot render a binding judgment; that mischaracterizes mediation; **D** arbitration can be binding, so calling it always advisory is incorrect.

questions.stem: A merchant emails another merchant a signed offer to sell goods and promises in writing to hold the offer open for 30 days, with no payment for that promise. Under UCC Article 2, when may the offeror revoke?

options.text: The offer is irrevocable for the stated time (up to three months) as a firm offer, even without consideration
Immediately, because no consideration supports the promise to keep it open
Only after the buyer pays for an option
Never, because all written offers are permanently irrevocable

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Under UCC 2-205, a merchant's signed written assurance to hold an offer open is a firm offer that is irrevocable for the stated period (not exceeding three months) without consideration. Why the others are wrong: **B** the firm-offer rule dispenses with the consideration requirement for merchants; **C** no option payment is needed for a UCC firm offer; **D** firm offers are irrevocable only for the stated time, capped at three months, not forever.

questions.stem: An aunt promises her nephew $1,000 as a birthday gift. The nephew gives nothing in return, and the aunt later refuses to pay. Is the promise enforceable as a contract?

options.text: No, because a gratuitous promise lacks consideration
Yes, because the promise was clearly stated
Yes, because family promises are always binding
No, because the amount was too small to enforce

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** A promise to make a gift is unenforceable because the promisee gives no bargained-for consideration in exchange. Why the others are wrong: **B** clarity of a promise does not supply the missing consideration; **C** family relationship does not make a gratuitous promise binding; **D** the defect is the absence of consideration, not the dollar amount.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old signs a contract to buy a used car (not a necessity). Before turning 18, the minor wants out of the deal. Under the general common-law rule, the contract is:

options.text: Void from the start and unenforceable by anyone
Voidable at the option of the minor, who may disaffirm it
Fully binding because the minor signed it
Binding only on the seller, never on the minor or the seller

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** A contract with a minor for a non-necessary is generally voidable by the minor, who may disaffirm during minority or shortly after reaching majority. Why the others are wrong: **A** the contract is voidable, not void, so it is not automatically a nullity; **C** the minor's lack of capacity lets the minor avoid it, so it is not fully binding on the minor; **D** the adult party is bound and cannot escape merely because the other party is a minor.

questions.stem: Two parties form a contract that expressly benefits a third person who is not a party, intending that the third person receive the performance. What is that third person called?

options.text: An intended third-party beneficiary who may enforce the contract
An incidental beneficiary with full enforcement rights
An assignor of the contract
A guarantor of both parties

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** An intended third-party beneficiary is one the contracting parties meant to benefit, and such a beneficiary may enforce the contract once rights vest. Why the others are wrong: **B** an incidental beneficiary benefits only by happenstance and cannot enforce the contract; **C** an assignor transfers rights it already holds, which is a different concept; **D** a guarantor promises to answer for another's debt, not a beneficiary designation.

questions.stem: A buyer breaches a contract to purchase goods. The seller resells them elsewhere at a lower price. What is the basic measure of the seller's expectation damages?

options.text: The amount needed to put the seller in the position it would have occupied had the contract been performed
The total revenue the seller hoped to earn that year
Punitive damages to punish the breaching buyer
Only the buyer's lost profits

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Expectation damages aim to give the non-breaching party the benefit of the bargain, putting it where it would have been had the contract been performed. Why the others are wrong: **B** hoped-for annual revenue is speculative and not the contract measure; **C** punitive damages are generally unavailable for ordinary breach of contract; **D** the buyer's lost profits are irrelevant to the seller's recovery.

questions.stem: In a general partnership, a partner signs a contract with a supplier in the ordinary course of the partnership's business. Who is liable on that contract?

options.text: Only the partner who signed it
The partnership and the partners, who are generally jointly and severally liable for partnership obligations
No one, because partnerships cannot contract
Only silent partners who did not sign

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** A partner has authority to bind the partnership on ordinary-course contracts, and partners are generally jointly and severally liable for partnership obligations. Why the others are wrong: **A** liability is not limited to the signing partner alone; the partnership and partners are bound; **C** partnerships can and do enter contracts through their partners; **D** all general partners share liability, not only silent ones.

questions.stem: A creditor of a corporation seeks to hold the sole shareholder personally liable, arguing the shareholder ignored corporate formalities, commingled funds, and left the company undercapitalized. What doctrine does the creditor invoke?

options.text: Piercing the corporate veil
The business judgment rule
Respondeat superior
The ultra vires doctrine

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Piercing the corporate veil lets a court disregard limited liability and reach a shareholder who abused the corporate form, as through commingling and undercapitalization. Why the others are wrong: **B** the business judgment rule shields good-faith director decisions; **C** respondeat superior holds an employer liable for an employee's torts; **D** ultra vires concerns acts beyond a corporation's chartered powers, not shareholder liability.

questions.stem: Which two contracts generally fall within the Statute of Frauds and must be evidenced by a signed writing to be enforceable? (Select two.)

options.text: A promise to answer for the debt of another (a suretyship)
A contract that by its terms cannot be performed within one year
A contract to sell a $50 textbook
An agreement to wash a car next Saturday

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** Suretyship promises and contracts not capable of performance within one year are classic Statute-of-Frauds categories requiring a signed writing. Why the others are wrong: **C** a sale of goods under $500 is below the UCC writing threshold; **D** a one-day service performable within a year need not be in writing.

questions.stem: A defendant is charged with a crime that requires proof he acted 'knowingly.' This element describes which component of criminal liability?

options.text: Mens rea (the required mental state)
Actus reus (the wrongful act)
Corpus delicti (the body of the crime)
Venue (the place of trial)

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Mens rea is the culpable mental state, such as acting knowingly, purposely, recklessly, or negligently. Why the others are wrong: **B** actus reus is the physical act or conduct element, not the mental state; **C** corpus delicti refers to proof that a crime occurred, not the mental element; **D** venue concerns where a case is tried, unrelated to the mental state.

questions.stem: Police arrest a suspect and begin custodial interrogation. To use the suspect's later statements in the prosecution's case-in-chief, what must the police generally have done first?

options.text: Provided Miranda warnings of the right to remain silent and to counsel
Obtained a search warrant for the suspect's home
Convened a grand jury
Allowed the suspect to post bail

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Statements from custodial interrogation are generally inadmissible in the case-in-chief unless the suspect first received Miranda warnings and validly waived those rights. Why the others are wrong: **B** a search warrant concerns searches, not the admissibility of interrogation statements; **C** a grand jury indicts but is not a prerequisite to Miranda; **D** bail relates to pretrial release, not the warnings required before questioning.

questions.stem: A testator wants to change one specific gift in an existing will without rewriting the entire document. What instrument accomplishes this?

options.text: A codicil
A living will
A power of attorney
A quitclaim deed

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** A codicil is a supplement that amends a will and must be executed with the same formalities as the will. Why the others are wrong: **B** a living will states end-of-life medical wishes, not testamentary gifts; **C** a power of attorney authorizes an agent to act during life and ends at death; **D** a quitclaim deed transfers real-property interests, not will provisions.

questions.stem: A settlor creates a trust during her lifetime and expressly reserves the power to amend or revoke it at any time. What type of trust is this?

options.text: A revocable (living) inter vivos trust
An irrevocable testamentary trust
A constructive trust imposed by a court
A resulting trust arising by operation of law

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** A trust created during life that the settlor may amend or revoke is a revocable living (inter vivos) trust. Why the others are wrong: **B** a testamentary trust arises under a will at death, and reserving a power to revoke makes it revocable, not irrevocable; **C** a constructive trust is an equitable remedy a court imposes to prevent unjust enrichment; **D** a resulting trust arises by implication of law, not by the settlor's express reserved power.

questions.stem: A homeowner gives a bank a security interest in real property to secure a loan, signing a document that allows the bank to foreclose on default. What is this instrument generally called?

options.text: A mortgage
A bill of sale
An easement appurtenant
A promissory estoppel

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** A mortgage is the instrument granting a lender a security interest in real property to secure repayment, with foreclosure available on default. Why the others are wrong: **B** a bill of sale transfers ownership of personal property; **C** an easement appurtenant is a right to use neighboring land, not loan security; **D** promissory estoppel is a contract doctrine, not a real-property security instrument.

questions.stem: A seller conveys land by a deed that promises the title is free of undisclosed encumbrances and that the grantor will defend the title against all claims. Which type of deed offers these broadest protections to the buyer?

options.text: A general warranty deed
A quitclaim deed
A bargain-and-sale deed without covenants
A sheriff's deed

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** A general warranty deed contains the fullest covenants of title and warrants against defects arising at any time, defending the grantee against all claims. Why the others are wrong: **B** a quitclaim deed conveys only whatever interest the grantor has, with no warranties; **C** a bargain-and-sale deed without covenants gives no title guarantees; **D** a sheriff's deed from an execution sale typically carries no general warranties.

questions.stem: A pedestrian is injured when a driver runs a red light. In the negligence claim, which element is satisfied by showing the driver's conduct was both the actual (but-for) cause and the proximate cause of the injury?

options.text: Duty
Breach
Causation
Damages

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Causation requires both actual cause (but-for) and proximate cause (a sufficiently close connection without a superseding event). Why the others are wrong: **A** duty is the obligation to exercise reasonable care, a separate element; **B** breach is the failure to meet the standard of care; **D** damages is the actual harm suffered, distinct from the causal link.

questions.stem: A keeper of a tiger that escapes and injures a neighbor is sued. Under the majority rule, on what basis is the keeper of such a wild animal generally liable?

options.text: Strict liability, regardless of how carefully the animal was kept
Only if the neighbor proves the keeper was negligent
Only if the keeper intended the harm
Never, because animals are not the owner's responsibility

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Owners of wild (non-domesticated) animals are strictly liable for harm caused by the animal's dangerous propensities, irrespective of care taken. Why the others are wrong: **B** strict liability applies, so proof of negligence is not required; **C** intent is not an element of this strict-liability theory; **D** the keeper is responsible for harm from a dangerous wild animal.

questions.stem: An unsecured creditor wants to collect on a past-due account, but the debtor has filed for bankruptcy. To pursue payment from the bankruptcy estate, what must the creditor generally file?

options.text: A proof of claim
A notice of appeal
A motion for summary judgment
A writ of certiorari

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** A creditor asserts its right to payment from the bankruptcy estate by timely filing a proof of claim. Why the others are wrong: **B** a notice of appeal challenges a ruling and does not assert a claim in bankruptcy; **C** a summary-judgment motion is a civil-litigation device, not the way to participate as a creditor; **D** a writ of certiorari seeks Supreme Court review, unrelated to filing a bankruptcy claim.

questions.stem: Trustees liquidate a Chapter 7 estate with limited funds. Under the Bankruptcy Code's priority scheme, how are creditors generally paid?

options.text: Secured creditors are paid from their collateral first, then priority unsecured claims, then general unsecured creditors
General unsecured creditors are always paid before secured creditors
Whichever creditor filed its lawsuit first is paid in full first
All creditors are paid in full regardless of available funds

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Secured creditors look first to their collateral, then statutory priority unsecured claims are paid, and general unsecured creditors share what remains pro rata. Why the others are wrong: **B** secured creditors generally have priority in their collateral over general unsecured creditors; **C** bankruptcy distribution follows the statutory priority scheme, not a race to the courthouse; **D** with limited funds, lower-priority creditors often receive only a fraction or nothing.

questions.stem: A defendant breaks into a neighbor's house at night intending to steal jewelry inside. Which crime most precisely describes the unlawful entry of a structure with intent to commit a crime inside?

options.text: Burglary
Robbery
Arson
Battery

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Burglary is the unlawful entry of a structure with the intent to commit a crime (such as theft) inside. Why the others are wrong: **B** robbery is taking property from a person by force or threat, not entry of a structure; **C** arson is the malicious burning of property; **D** battery is harmful or offensive contact with a person.

questions.stem: A widow's husband dies leaving a will that disinherits her entirely. Under the majority approach in common-law (non-community-property) states, what protection is typically available to the surviving spouse?

options.text: An elective (forced) share of the deceased spouse's estate
Nothing, because a will always controls completely
Automatic ownership of all of the decedent's property
A criminal claim against the estate's executor

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Most separate-property states give a disinherited surviving spouse the right to claim an elective (forced) share of the estate, overriding the will to that extent. Why the others are wrong: **B** the elective share is an exception to a will's control, so it does not always govern completely; **C** the spouse receives a statutory share, not automatically all of the property; **D** disinheritance is not a crime and gives no criminal claim against the executor.

questions.stem: Which two of the following are generally classified as felonies rather than misdemeanors? (Select two.)

options.text: Murder
Aggravated robbery
A minor traffic infraction
Simple disorderly conduct punishable by a small fine

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** Felonies are serious crimes generally punishable by more than a year of imprisonment, such as murder and aggravated robbery. Why the others are wrong: **C** a minor traffic infraction is a petty offense, not a felony; **D** disorderly conduct punishable by a small fine is a misdemeanor or lesser offense, not a felony.

questions.stem: Which two interests are non-possessory rights in another person's land rather than possessory estates? (Select two.)

options.text: An easement
A restrictive covenant
A fee simple absolute
A life estate

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** An easement (a right to use) and a restrictive covenant (a promise restricting land use) are non-possessory interests in another's land. Why the others are wrong: **C** a fee simple absolute is the most complete possessory ownership estate; **D** a life estate is a possessory estate measured by a life, not a non-possessory interest.

questions.stem: Place the following stages of a typical felony criminal case in the correct chronological order, from earliest to latest.

options.text: Arrest
Arraignment
Trial
Sentencing

questions.explanation: A felony case typically begins with the arrest (A) of the suspect on probable cause. The defendant is then brought before the court for arraignment (B), where charges are read and a plea is entered. If the case is not resolved by plea, it proceeds to trial (C), where guilt is determined. Upon a conviction, the court imposes punishment at sentencing (D). This arrest-to-arraignment-to-trial-to-sentencing progression reflects the standard order of criminal proceedings.

questions.stem: A party who lost in a federal court of appeals asks the U.S. Supreme Court to hear the case. What is the discretionary order by which the Supreme Court agrees to review the decision?

options.text: A writ of mandamus
A writ of certiorari
A writ of habeas corpus
A writ of attachment

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** The Supreme Court exercises most of its appellate review through the discretionary writ of certiorari, granting review of only a small fraction of petitions. Why the others are wrong: **A** a writ of mandamus orders a lower court or official to perform a duty; **C** a writ of habeas corpus tests the legality of a person's detention; **D** a writ of attachment is a prejudgment device to seize property to secure a claim.

questions.stem: A federal court sits in diversity to decide a state-law negligence claim. On the substantive standard of care, which body of law must the federal court apply?

options.text: Federal common law fashioned by the court
The substantive law of the relevant state
Whatever rule the federal judge believes is best
The law of the state with the most residents

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Under the Erie doctrine, a federal court sitting in diversity applies state substantive law (while following federal procedural law). Why the others are wrong: **A** Erie rejected a general federal common law for state-law claims; **C** the judge may not substitute a preferred rule for the governing state law; **D** the applicable state is determined by choice-of-law rules, not by population.

questions.stem: Two businesses disagree about whether a contract clause permits a planned course of action, but neither has yet breached. One asks a court to declare the parties' rights under the contract before anyone acts. What kind of relief is this?

options.text: A summary judgment
A default judgment
A declaratory judgment
A consent decree

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** A declaratory judgment lets a court declare the parties' legal rights and relationships before any breach or further harm occurs. Why the others are wrong: **B** a default judgment is entered when a party fails to respond or appear; **A** a summary judgment resolves a case on the merits when there is no genuine factual dispute; **D** a consent decree is a court-approved settlement, not a judicial declaration of disputed rights.

questions.stem: A taxpayer files suit challenging a federal statute that has been enacted but will not take effect or affect anyone for several years, and no enforcement is threatened. A court is most likely to decline to hear the case on what ground?

options.text: The claim is not ripe for adjudication
The claim is moot
The doctrine of stare decisis bars it
The claim presents diversity jurisdiction

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Ripeness bars suits brought too early, where the harm is contingent or speculative and no concrete dispute yet exists. Why the others are wrong: **B** mootness applies when a once-live controversy has already ended, the opposite timing problem; **C** stare decisis concerns following precedent, not whether a dispute is justiciable; **D** diversity jurisdiction is a basis for hearing a case, not a reason to dismiss one.

questions.stem: A federal agency issues a regulation. A challenger argues the rule is invalid because it exceeds what Congress authorized. The scope of an agency's rulemaking power is fixed primarily by what?

options.text: The preferences of the regulated industry
The agency's internal staff manual
A press release from the agency head
The agency's enabling (organic) statute

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** An agency may act only within the authority delegated by its enabling statute; a rule exceeding that grant is invalid. Why the others are wrong: **B** an internal staff manual guides employees but does not expand statutory authority; **C** a press release does not confer legal rulemaking power; **A** the regulated industry's wishes do not define the agency's lawful authority.

questions.stem: Which two requirements must a plaintiff generally satisfy to have constitutional standing to sue in federal court? (Select two.)

options.text: A concrete and particularized injury in fact
An injury fairly traceable to the defendant's conduct that a favorable ruling would likely redress
Residency in the same state as the court
A general interest in seeing the law obeyed

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** Standing requires an injury in fact that is concrete and particularized, plus causation (traceable to the defendant) and redressability. Why the others are wrong: **C** residency relates to venue or jurisdiction, not standing; **D** a generalized grievance shared by the public at large does not confer standing.

questions.stem: A solo attorney wants to pay a paralegal a percentage of the legal fees earned on the matters the paralegal works on. Under the ABA Model Rules, is this arrangement permissible?

options.text: Yes, because the paralegal is supervised
Yes, as long as the paralegal is competent
No, a lawyer generally may not share legal fees with a nonlawyer
Yes, provided the client signs a waiver

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Model Rule 5.4 prohibits sharing legal fees with nonlawyers to protect professional independence; a paralegal may be paid a salary or bonus but not a cut of legal fees. Why the others are wrong: **B** competence does not authorize fee splitting; **A** supervision does not cure the prohibition; **D** a client waiver cannot override the rule against nonlawyer fee sharing.

questions.stem: A law firm receives a $5,000 advance from a client to cover future fees and costs not yet earned or incurred. Under the ABA Model Rules, where must the firm deposit those funds?

options.text: In the firm's general operating account
In a separate client trust account, not the firm's operating account
In the supervising partner's personal account
In a petty-cash drawer at the office

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Model Rule 1.15 requires unearned fees and client funds to be held in a separate client trust account and kept apart from the lawyer's own property. Why the others are wrong: **A** placing unearned client money in the operating account is improper commingling; **C** depositing it in a personal account is commingling and risks conversion; **D** holding client funds in petty cash fails the safekeeping and separation requirements.

questions.stem: An attorney formerly represented a client in negotiating a commercial lease. The attorney is now asked to represent a new client suing the former client to void that same lease. Absent informed consent, what does the conflict rule require?

options.text: The conflict disappears once one year has passed
The attorney may proceed because the prior representation has ended
The attorney may proceed if the new client pays a higher fee
The attorney must decline, because the new matter is substantially related and materially adverse to the former client

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** Model Rule 1.9 bars representation adverse to a former client in the same or a substantially related matter without the former client's informed consent. Why the others are wrong: **B** the duty to a former client survives the end of the engagement; **C** a larger fee does not cure a former-client conflict; **A** there is no automatic time limit that dissolves the duty.

questions.stem: A paralegal communicates with clients and third parties by email and on the firm's letterhead. Under the rules and guidelines on holding out, what must be clear about the paralegal's status?

options.text: The paralegal's nonlawyer status must be disclosed so no one is misled into thinking the paralegal is an attorney
The paralegal may use the title 'Esquire' if approved by the supervising attorney
The paralegal need not disclose status to existing clients
The paralegal may imply attorney status as long as work is supervised

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** A paralegal must disclose nonlawyer status so clients, courts, and the public are not misled into believing the paralegal is a lawyer. Why the others are wrong: **B** 'Esquire' designates a lawyer and is improper for a paralegal; **C** status must be clear to all, including existing clients; **D** implying attorney status is a misrepresentation even when the work is supervised.

questions.stem: Under the Model Rules, which two circumstances generally require or permit an attorney to withdraw from representing a client? (Select two.)

options.text: Continuing the representation would require the lawyer to violate the rules or the law (mandatory withdrawal)
The client insists on pursuing a clearly fraudulent course of conduct
The client asks a difficult but lawful legal question
Opposing counsel requests that the lawyer step aside

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** A lawyer must withdraw when continuing would violate the rules or law, and may withdraw when the client persists in fraudulent or criminal conduct. Why the others are wrong: **C** a hard but lawful question is part of ordinary representation, not a basis for withdrawal; **D** opposing counsel cannot force a lawyer off a case by mere request.

questions.stem: A plaintiff files a state-law claim in state court against a defendant from another state, and the case satisfies the federal diversity requirements. The defendant would prefer to litigate in federal court. What procedure allows the defendant to move the case there?

options.text: Interpleader
A motion for a new trial
Removal to federal court
A motion to certify a class

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** A defendant may remove a case from state to federal court when the federal court would have had original jurisdiction, such as through diversity. Why the others are wrong: **B** a motion for a new trial is a post-trial device, not a way to change courts; **A** interpleader resolves competing claims to the same stake; **D** class certification concerns whether a case may proceed as a class action, not removal.

questions.stem: At a civil trial, a party wishes to call a witness to give an opinion based on specialized engineering knowledge. Under the Federal Rules of Evidence, such expert opinion testimony is admissible only if, among other things:

options.text: The witness personally witnessed the events in dispute
The witness is qualified by knowledge, skill, experience, training, or education and the testimony is reliable and helpful
The witness is related to one of the parties
The opinion is based solely on the witness's gut feeling
